sections.title: As It Absorbs, So It Expels
sections.html:
As we have learned (above 32:1), the fundamental rule in the laws of kashering utensils is: ke-bol'o kakh polto (“as it absorbs, so it expels”) – the way a utensil was used with a forbidden substance determines the way it is kashered. There are three types of kashering: a) rinsing; b) hagala (purging in boiling water);
c) libun (heating to incandescence in fire). Let us explain further: the first type is rinsing in water, which is the lightest kashering, intended for utensils used with cold forbidden foods; to kasher them, one must rinse them in water and clean them of the remnants of the forbidden food that remained stuck to their walls. The second type is hagala in boiling water, intended for utensils in which forbidden foods were cooked. The word hagala denotes expulsion, for putting the utensil into boiling water makes it expel the flavors that were absorbed and stuck to it through cooking. The third type is libun in ur (fire), intended for utensils used directly in fire, such as skewers and grilling grates.1

The difference between the three types of kashering is as follows. When utensils were used cold, the remnants of the foods stick to the utensils externally, and rinsing washes them off and kashers them. When utensils were used for cooking, the cooking causes the flavors of the foods to stick to and be absorbed in the utensils more strongly, so rinsing will not help them, and only hagala in boiling water, which melts the fats and expels the flavors that stuck to and were absorbed in the utensil, can kasher them. And when utensils were used in fire (ur), for roasting or baking, the flavors stick to and are absorbed in the utensils with great force and in a harder manner than in cooking, because cooking is done with liquids that soften the absorption and sticking of the flavors. In addition, cooking is generally done at a heat that does not exceed one hundred degrees, because the liquids in the cooking moderate the rise in heat, whereas baking and roasting, which are done without liquids, are done at higher heat. Therefore hagala in boiling water can expel only part of the flavors that stuck to and were absorbed in the utensil through fire, and to eliminate them one must perform libun on the utensil in fire, which will burn and consume the flavors absorbed in the baking pan or the skewer. It emerges that, as a rule, hagala expels and removes the flavor stuck to and absorbed in the utensil, whereas libun burns the flavor while it is still in it.

sections.title: The Levels of Hagala
sections.html:
The obligation of hagala follows the level of use of the utensil; there are four levels: a) a keli rishon (primary vessel) on the fire; b) a keli rishon that is not on the fire;
c) irui (pouring) from a keli rishon; d) a keli sheni (secondary vessel).

A keli rishon is the pot in which one cooks on the fire, as well as a spoon with which one stirs a dish cooking on the fire. If the dish was non-kosher, they are kashered the way they absorbed – in boiling water in a keli rishon on the fire.

A keli rishon that is not on the fire is a pot that was on the fire and was removed from it, or under which the fire was turned off. Since it is no longer being heated on the fire, its heat weakens and it lacks the power to cook and cause flavors to be absorbed as when it was on the fire. Therefore, if a spoon was put into it, the spoon can be kashered in a keli rishon that is not on the fire, provided that the water in it is still very hot.

Irui: A bowl into which a non-kosher dish was poured from a keli rishon – since the non-kosher dish has been disconnected from the pot in which it was heated, it cannot cause flavors to be absorbed and to stick to the same degree as a keli rishon, and therefore it suffices to kasher the bowl by pouring very hot water over it from a keli rishon.

A keli sheni is the vessel into which the dish was poured from the keli rishon. If, for example, boiling water was poured into a keli sheni, and non-kosher meat was put into it to be heated in that water, the vessel requires kashering at the level of a keli sheni. Admittedly, many are lenient and hold that a keli sheni does not absorb and does not require kashering; however, since there are those who are stringent, one should perform hagala on a keli sheni as well.

A dish in a keli rishon that cooled down until its heat fell below 45 degrees cannot cook and cause flavors to be absorbed; therefore, if a spoon was put into it, the spoon does not require hagala, and it suffices to kasher it by rinsing.

Non-kosher dishes that are in a keli shelishi (tertiary vessel), even though they are very hot, since they have already moved far from the source of heat, are not considered to cause flavors to be absorbed or expelled; therefore the utensils that came into contact with them do not require kashering by hagala, and it suffices to kasher them by rinsing.2

A knife with which one cut boiling non-kosher meat on the fire requires libun. If one cut the meat after it was removed from the fire, the knife requires hagala. Likewise, a fork stuck into a non-kosher baked item while it was in the oven requires libun; if after it was taken out of the oven, it requires hagala.

Regarding cold non-kosher soup that remained in a utensil for a full day, some say the utensil requires hagala, based on the rule that kavush ke-mevushal (“soaked is like cooked”). And this is the practice to rule le-khatḥila (ab initio). In time of need, one may be lenient and kasher glass and metal utensils by rinsing, since it is known that they do not absorb (below 35:9; Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 10:13).

Many are accustomed le-khatḥila to kasher all the utensils that require hagala in a keli rishon, that is, in boiling water on the fire, because they are concerned that perhaps the utensils were used in a keli rishon and this was forgotten (see Rema OḤ 451:6; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 107). However, when the level of the forbidden use is clear, there is no need to kasher the utensil at a higher level.

sections.title: A Utensil Used at Different Levels
sections.html:
The poskim disagree about how to kasher a utensil that was used with non-kosher food at different levels of use, such as a fork that is usually used with cold foods that are not hot enough to scald the hand (yad soledet bo), whose kashering is by rinsing, but is sometimes used with scalding-hot dishes, whose kashering is by hagala, and rarely is used for roasting, whose kashering is by libun.

Some say that it must be kashered according to its most severe use, for since it absorbed at a severe level of absorption, it must be kashered at that level. And some say that it must be kashered according to its majority use, and one need not be concerned about the severe absorption, because in practice after a full day the flavor absorbed in the utensil is already spoiled and cannot render foods forbidden. Nevertheless, one must still kasher a utensil that was used with non-kosher food, and the obligation is determined by the majority of the forbidden uses made of it.

Le-khatḥila one should be stringent and kasher the utensil according to its most severe use; and in time of need, when it is difficult to kasher the utensil according to its most severe use, one may be lenient and kasher it according to its majority use. For example, a utensil whose kashering according to its most severe use would require libun, which might damage it, may be kashered by hagala according to its majority use.3

Majority and minority in this matter are determined only according to the forbidden uses. For example, a fork with which one usually eats non-kosher food cold, and once stirred non-kosher food with it in a keli rishon – its kashering follows its majority use, by rinsing. But if it is a fork with which one always eats kosher foods cold, and once stirred non-kosher food with it in a keli rishon on the fire – its kashering is by hagala in a keli rishon, since only the use in the keli rishon was a forbidden use that requires kashering.4

sections.title: Preparing Utensils for Hagala, and Kashering Pots
sections.html:
One must clean the utensil before kashering it by hagala, because the boiling water removes the flavors absorbed in and stuck to the utensil, but does not clean the utensil of all the food remnants stuck to it. One who kashered a utensil by hagala without first cleaning it must clean it and perform hagala again (SA OḤ 451:3).

The handles of utensils must also be kashered, because in metal utensils, when the body of the utensil is heated, the heat also spreads to its handles, and if they reach a heat of yad soledet bo, the entire utensil, including its handles, is considered a utensil that was used with a forbidden substance, and all of it requires kashering. Wooden handles must also be kashered, for although they do not get so hot, sometimes the dish boils over or splatters onto them and its flavor is absorbed in and sticks to them (SA OḤ 451:12; MB 68). However, since the use and absorption of the handles is not as severe as that of a keli rishon on the fire, they can be kashered by irui from a keli rishon (Rema ibid.). When the handles of pots can be removed, some are mehadrin (meticulous) to remove them and clean them before the hagala. Instead, one may clean around them with plenty of soap, until it is clear that the food remnants that may have remained there have been spoiled.

Likewise, a utensil that has grooves from which it is difficult to remove food remnants must be cleaned with plenty of soap, until it is clear that the food remnants in the grooves have been spoiled, and afterwards one performs hagala on the utensil.

The hagala of a pot must be carried out inside a large vessel into which it can be entirely inserted. One should not suffice with boiling water inside the pot, because it is reasonable to assume that over the many times it was used, the dish boiled over or splattered from it onto the rim of the utensil, and then the forbidden flavor was absorbed in and stuck to the upper rim of the pot as well, and the rim of the pot is not kashered by boiling water inside the pot. When there is no large vessel in which the pot can be kashered, one should fill the pot one wishes to kasher with water and bring it to a boil, and at the same time boil water in a small vessel; when the water inside the pot boils, one puts the small vessel into it, and this will cause a lot of water to overflow and spill over the sides of the pot and kasher its rim (see Avoda Zara 76a; and see SA 452:6).5

sections.title: Waiting Twenty-Four Hours Before Hagala
sections.html:
The custom is not to perform hagala on utensils that are benei yoman, that is, within twenty-four hours of their being used with a forbidden substance. This is because during a full day the flavor absorbed in and stuck to the utensil is still good, and if the hagala water does not contain sixty times the thickness of the utensil's walls, the water might take on the forbidden flavor and cause it to stick to and be absorbed in the utensil's walls again, and it would turn out that the hagala was ineffective. But after a full day, the flavor that was absorbed in and stuck to the utensil has become spoiled, and then even if the hagala water does not contain sixty times the utensil, the utensil will be kashered, because then the utensil expels a spoiled flavor into the water, and even if it reabsorbs from it, it does not become forbidden. For only if the flavor that was originally absorbed was good does the utensil remain in its forbidden state even after the flavor becomes spoiled; but if at the time the flavor was absorbed in and stuck to the utensil it was spoiled – the utensil does not become forbidden.

There is a further concern: if meat and dairy utensils are kashered in the same water, a good meat flavor and a good dairy flavor will be expelled into the hagala water, and if the hagala water does not contain sixty times more than one of them, the flavors will not be nullified in sixty and will mix with each other and render forbidden the hagala water and the utensils kashered in it, because they will absorb meat and dairy flavor together. But after a full day, the meat and dairy flavors expelled from the utensils will be spoiled and will not render the hagala water and the utensils forbidden, because noten ta'am li-fgam (a flavor that imparts a detrimental taste) is permitted (SA OḤ 452:2, MB ibid.).

In public hagala stations, the custom is not to rely on those coming to kasher to have left their utensils for a full day before the hagala, and in order to avoid mishaps, liquid soap is added to the hagala water; thereby any flavor expelled from the utensils is immediately spoiled, and even if it is reabsorbed in the utensils, since it is spoiled it does not render the utensils forbidden. Likewise, when one wishes to kasher utensils by hagala without waiting a full day, one may put liquid soap into the water and kasher them le-khatḥila within a full day.6

sections.title: Performing the Hagala in Practice
sections.html:
Any of the kitchen pots may be used for the hagala, provided that it is clean. The hagala water must be boiling. In time of need, when soap is mixed into the hagala water, one may even boil the hagala water in a non-kosher pot, for since the flavor of the water is spoiled, the non-kosher utensil does not render the hagala water forbidden (although the pot itself has not been kashered, as explained above, section 4).

One leaves the utensil in the boiling water for about three seconds. Le-khatḥila, after the hagala the custom is to rinse the utensil in cold water, but this is not indispensable. Therefore, when it is difficult to rinse in cold water – there is no obligation to take the trouble to do so (SA OḤ 452:7; MB 34).7

Sometimes putting the utensils in cools the water slightly until it stops boiling, and then one must leave the utensils in the water until it returns to a boil; the sign of this is that it produces bubbles.

A utensil that cannot be put entirely into the water may be kashered first one half and afterwards the other half (SA 451:11).

When one must kasher many utensils, such as cutlery, it is convenient to put them in a basket into the boiling water, and after leaving them for about three seconds, to take the basket out of the water, and the utensils are kosher. Since there is a concern that the utensils will be pressed against each other and the boiling water will not pass between them, one should shake the basket a little in the water so that the boiling water enters between the utensils and kashers them (based on SA OḤ 452:3-4).

One may kasher utensils without a basket by dropping the utensil into the boiling water, for while the utensil sinks in the boiling water, the water surrounds it on all sides and kashers it. If one needs to kasher several utensils, such as cutlery, one should drop them into the water one after another. If one wishes to fulfill the custom of rinsing them in cold water immediately after their kashering, one should pour out the boiling water and drop the kashered utensils into a vessel of cold water. However, as we have learned, there is no obligation to do so, and one may wait until the boiling water cools and then take out of it the utensils that have already been kashered.

In summary, this is the order of hagala: one cleans the utensil, boils water in a large, clean vessel, puts the utensil requiring hagala into the boiling water, sees that the water continues to boil, and after about three seconds takes out the kashered utensil. The custom is to add soapy water to the hagala water or to wait a full day between the forbidden use and the hagala. Le-khatḥila, one rinses the utensil in cold water after the hagala.

sections.title: Libun
sections.html:
Utensils whose use is in ur (fire), such as skewers and baking pans, are kashered by libun. It makes no difference whether the heat source is actual fire or electric heating coils and the like; whenever forbidden food was roasted or baked in them, they must be kashered by libun.

The Sages said that libun is putting the utensil into fire until “its peel falls off” (Bavli Avoda Zara 76a), or until sparks come out of it (Yerushalmi Avoda Zara 5:15). Since generally the iron itself does not peel and does not emit sparks in fire, it seems that the Sages' intent is that the libun will cause the foods stuck to the utensil to peel off it, or sparks to fly from them. The question is at what heat the utensil reaches this.

Many hold that the libun must be at a heat that burns and makes the metal glow, until all the food remnants that stuck to and were absorbed in the utensil are burned. This heat is about 350 degrees to about 400 degrees. And even though the fire on which the forbidden food was roasted or baked did not reach such a heat, in their opinion only when the utensil glows in the fire will all the forbidden flavors that stuck to and were absorbed in it be burned.

Some are lenient and hold that the rule ke-bol'o kakh polto applies to the heat of the fire as well, so that at the same heat at which the forbidden flavor stuck to and was absorbed in the utensil, it can be kashered. If its use was at a heat of 200 degrees – it can be kashered at 200 degrees. In their opinion, a baking pan in which forbidden food was baked in an oven can be kashered at the heat of that same oven.

In practice, the prevalent custom follows the stringent opinion, and since the pan is liable to be damaged by such libun, one should not kasher a baking pan. For this is the rule: any utensil that is liable to be damaged by kashering is not kashered, lest people be negligent in kashering it so as not to damage it (see above 32:4). However, in a case of great loss one may be lenient and perform libun at the heat at which the forbidden substance was used, in accordance with the lenient opinion.

Therefore, one should not kasher baking pans in which non-kosher food was baked, since severe libun is liable to ruin them. But one who has great difficulty buying new pans, either because their cost is high for him or because it is hard for him to obtain them, may kasher them by heating them in that same oven at the highest heat for about half an hour. The same applies to a sir pele (“wonder pot”) and a Teflon frying pan.8

sections.title: Intermediate Cases Between Hagala and Libun
sections.html:
The difference between pots intended for cooking, whose kashering is by hagala in boiling water, and pans and skewers intended for baking and roasting, whose kashering is by libun, is that cooking is done with liquids that soften the dish, and therefore the remnants of the dish stick to and are absorbed in the utensil in a soft manner; whereas the aim of baking and roasting is to reduce the liquids in the foods and harden them, and consequently the food remnants stick to and are absorbed in the utensil in a hard manner. And even though baking pans are greased with oil, their kashering is by libun, since the oil is intended to prevent sticking and not to soften the baked item.

If non-kosher food that dried out was cooked in a pot, even though at the end of the cooking there was no longer liquid in the pot, its kashering is by hagala, since the beginning of its absorption was through liquids. Moreover, one follows the general purpose of the utensil, which is intended for cooking and not for baking (Rosh).

Accordingly, a frying pan is kashered by hagala, for the oil put in the frying pan is intended to add moisture to the food. This is the difference between baking and frying: baking dries out the baked item, whereas frying moistens the food. This is the view of most Rishonim (Rosh, Ra'avya, Mordekhai and Sha'arei Dura).

And some say that a frying pan is kashered by libun, for since people commonly fry in a frying pan even with a little oil, it often happens that the oil runs out and the absorption becomes dry, through fire. Furthermore, sometimes from the start there are places in the frying pan that have no oil, and the absorption there is through fire; therefore the law of the frying pan is like that of a baking pan, and its kashering is by libun (Rashba and Rabbeinu Yoel).

In practice, one should kasher a frying pan by libun kal, that is, heating the frying pan on the stovetop until, if paper were placed on the frying pan, it would be singed, or if a thin thread were stretched across its rim, it would be singed and tear from the great heat. For in this way its kashering is in the manner of its use. This is also convenient for kashering it, since it involves heating the empty frying pan on the same fire on which one usually fries.9

sections.title: Meat and Dairy Baking Pans That Were Mixed Up
sections.html:
If a clean meat baking pan was used for a dairy baked item or vice versa, since in practice the meat and dairy flavors did not mix together, the pan can be kashered by hagala, in accordance with the law of heteira bela (explained in the note). All the more so it can be kashered by libun kal, by heating it in the oven at the highest heat for half an hour, for according to some poskim this kashering is considered full libun, which is effective even for absorption of a forbidden substance (as explained in halakha 7).10

Likewise, when one wishes to convert a pan from meat to dairy or vice versa, it suffices to kasher it by hagala or by heating it in the oven at the highest heat.

However, many in Ashkenaz were accustomed not to convert meat utensils to dairy and vice versa by hagala, so that people would not become confused and forget what was dairy and what was meat; but in time of need they were accustomed to be lenient. And in the other communities they ruled that one may perform hagala on a utensil in order to use it for the other kind for any purpose whatsoever, but they were not accustomed to do so frequently, so as not to create confusion in the kitchen between dairy and meat.11

sections.title: A Guide to Kashering a Non-Kosher Kitchen
sections.html:
Sink and countertop: One must clean them well, paying attention to the grooves, so that no food residue remains in them. Afterwards one must pour boiling water over the sink and its walls and over the entire countertop surface. Before the pouring, one must make sure the sink and countertop are dry, so that the boiling water will be poured directly onto them and not be cooled by the water on them. In a home kitchen it is customary to kasher the sink and countertop with water heated in an electric kettle, and since the water in the kettle is not enough to kasher the sinks and the whole countertop, the kashering is carried out in stages, where at each stage one pours the water boiled in the kettle over another area; and if the poured water flowed to a part that has not yet been kashered, one must sweep it away from there before pouring additional water boiled in the kettle over it. Therefore, one who wishes to save time in the kashering process should first pour over the bottom of the sink, then over its four walls, then begin to kasher the places adjacent to the sink, and from there continue gradually to the more distant places. Cleaning with a high-quality steam cleaner is as effective as pouring.

A delicate countertop that is liable to be damaged by pouring boiling water is kashered by rinsing and good cleaning (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 11:1-2).

Stovetop: Le-khatḥila, one should clean the stovetop and perform libun kal on the grate. When it is difficult to perform libun on the grate, one may suffice with cleaning the grate and performing hagala on it in boiling water; and when the grate is longer than the depth of the pot, one should first insert one side and afterwards the other side. The other iron parts of the grate that do not touch the pots, as well as the enamel surface under the grate and the gas burner heads, must be cleaned well of all food residue, but since these parts do not come into contact with the pots, there is no need to perform libun or hagala on them. Le-khatḥila, it is good to light all the burners for about a quarter of an hour (see Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 11:2, note 2).

Electric stovetop: One cleans it well and heats it at high heat for about a quarter of an hour, and ke-bol'o kakh polto. The same law applies to a ceramic stovetop, which looks like opaque glass, on which the pots are placed directly. Induction stovetop: One cleans the surface and pours boiling water over it, and heats pots on it for about a quarter of an hour, so that they will heat the surface under them in the manner of their use (see above 25, note 14).

Cutlery and pots: One first cleans them, fills a large pot with water, brings it to a boil and mixes soapy water into it in order to spoil its taste. While the water is boiling, one puts the cutlery into it, one utensil after another, and thereby kashers the cutlery. Likewise, one puts in the small pots that can fit into it, and thereby kashers them. The kashering of the large pot and of pots that do not fit into it was explained in halakha 4.

Baking oven: One cleans the oven of food remnants and operates it at the highest heat for about half an hour, and thereby the body of the oven is kashered. Baking pans are not kashered, since according to most poskim they must be kashered by severe libun, and this is liable to damage them. In a case of great loss, for example when there is no way to obtain new pans or their price is high, they may be kashered by heating them in the oven at the highest heat for about half an hour (above halakha 7 and note 8).

Microwave: It should be kashered in three stages: a) one cleans the food residue that may have remained in it due to boiling over and splatters; b) one performs hagala on the rotating plate in boiling water; c) one places in it a small dish of water with soap and heats it for about ten minutes at the highest heat, and thereby kashers it from the vapors and condensation that stuck to and were absorbed in it during its use with non-kosher food.

Dishwasher: One cleans the filter of the food remnants in it and runs the dishwasher at the highest heat, and thereby kashers the dishwasher and the racks together (see Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 11, note 5).

Table: If it is delicate and boiling pots are not placed on it, it suffices to clean it well with soap and water. If it is not delicate and boiling pots are sometimes placed on it, one should clean it and afterwards pour boiling water over it.

Refrigerator and cabinets: They are kashered by thorough cleaning with soap and water, in order to remove any sauce residue that may have stuck to them.

Mixer and blender: If they were used with cold foods, they are kashered by cleaning with soap and water alone. If they were used with boiling foods, they are kashered by hagala.

sections.title: Using a Non-Kosher Kitchen and Barbecue
sections.html:
As we have learned (32:3), it is forbidden to use utensils that require kashering for hot foods, for since forbidden foods were cooked in them, the Torah commanded that they be kashered. Now we will add that le-khatḥila one also should not use them for cold foods, even on an occasional basis. And one also should not use meat utensils for cold dairy foods or vice versa.

However, in a pressing situation, such as one who has arrived at a guesthouse (tzimmer) and has no kosher utensils and no possibility of kashering the non-kosher utensils, he may occasionally use clean meat utensils for cold dairy foods or vice versa. Likewise, in a pressing situation it is permitted to use clean non-kosher utensils for cold foods, dry and liquid, such as plates for salad, cups for cold drinks, teaspoons for eating yogurt and cheese, and soup bowls for milk with cereal. This is because as long as the utensils are clean and one eats cold foods in them, they do not cause flavors to be absorbed into the foods.12

When one wishes to use a barbecue grill, since the food touches the grate directly, one must kasher it. And since its use is in fire, its kashering is also in fire, and one must make sure that the fire reaches all parts of the grate, as it could have reached them when it was used with non-kosher food. There is no need to clean the grate, for since it is kashered by severe libun, all the foods stuck to it are burned and become completely unfit to be food.
